title: Canto Three. Childhood
html:
Crying stilled by Hari's name; the Infant eats clay; the pilgrim brahmin; the thief; pranks; striking His mother and the coconut; the girls at the Ganga and the meeting with Lakshmi; "there is no pure and impure"; the father's anger and Mishra's dream (pp. 15–19)

[p. 15]

1The boy, indulging in childish pranks, fondled by the women, by His antics intoxicated the hearts of those who watched Him, shedding tears of joy.

2If Mishra's son cried and no toy could console Him, the women would begin to chant the names of Hari — and He would start to dance and stop crying.1

3Once He, with His row of tender little teeth, was playing in the courtyard with all the boys; His mother, seeing the little one eating clay,

4held Him back, shook her finger at Him, scolded Him and said: "Ah, what recklessness! What do You want, child, why do You eat this nasty clay?

5In my house there are many foods made of cream and sugar; why have You given them up as if they were bitter? Ah, where has Your good sense gone!"

6Hearing His mother's words, the Lord, with a look of mingled fear and surprise, said to her: "Mother, what you tell Me is not false, but consider a child's words.

7All this food is only earth; taste is present in all things. Is not everything one at its root? Why then do you divide [things] into edible and inedible?"

8Amazed at the child's speech, that jewel among women said to Him: "If all food here is earth, still one kind is wholesome and another harmful.

9Payasa and the like nourish, while clay and the like cause grave illness. Therefore, son, people, after due thought, eat what is wholesome and sweet, not what is harmful.

10A living being lives in a healthy body that grows by wholesome food; otherwise it quickly wastes away. Look, dear one, at an example:

11in a very smooth clay pot water stays pure for a long time; but if it gets into a lump of clay, it quickly dries up and is seen no more."

12Hari, wishing to conceal Himself, approved His mother's words and said: "Mother, why didn't you tell Me this before? Now I won't eat it."

13Saying this, the golden beauty [Gaura], in the presence of the town women, began to drink at His mother's breast; and Shachi, taking in the child's words, rejoiced in her astonished heart.2

14Once a certain brahmin guest, tormented by hunger, asked her for cooked rice; and Shachi gladly gave the twice-born all he needed for cooking.

15He cooked the rice and, as he first began to offer it to Vishnu, the Lord in a trice ate the rice, vegetables and the rest — and laughed.

[p. 16]

16Seeing such strange behaviour in a child, [the brahmin] again with difficulty, keeping calm, cooked rice with vegetables — and the Lord again ate it all before his eyes.

17Then the brahmin, after chasing Him away many times and making sure He was sitting on His mother's lap, cooked again in agitation and offered it to the Lord.

18And at once, seeing Him eating the rice with a joyful face, he said: "Well! What a small tummy You have, child, yet it is never filled with this food!

19Mothers in the world gladly and happily feed many children; ah, what is this: with all her wealth she cannot feed one child!"

20Hearing these words, He was amused and, wishing to elevate this [brahmin] devoted to Vedic rites, at once disclosed His position and said to the brahmin, who shone with spiritual power:

21"I am not a hungry brahmin, nor is My stomach so very large; but what My devotee offers Me again and again I cannot let go by, even if it is a trifle."

22Having spoken this nectarean speech, the Lord, rejoicing, revealed Himself before him in the form that stirs Gokula — the colour of a raincloud, with a flute in His hands.

23Beholding Him with his own eyes, praising Him with beautiful words and bowing down, the brahmin partook of His remnants and at once attained the fulfilment of all aims.3

24One night, when His family were asleep, a certain thief, greedy for gold ornaments, carried off the Lotus-eyed One and ran away, hiding his steps.

25The people searching the house did not find the child in the inner room; their feet slipped on their tears, and at every step blinding grief overtook them.

26Gaurachandra, seeing His relatives in despair and Himself carried off by the thief for gain, made the thief feel His power and stole away his mind.

27And the thief, having wandered long and no longer able to carry the heavy burden, in the morning entered in amazement Mishra's house, full of cries of grief.

28The face of the child, sitting on the high shoulder of the thief, who stood stock-still, was like a reflection in a mirror set in a pillar — and became for the people a source of blessing.

29Shachi, beside herself with joy, pressing to her heart the son who had returned as if from the dead, let even the thief go in peace and spoke not one harsh, angry word to him.4

30With a band of strong boys He would enter the houses of the townsfolk like a thief, smash the pots and eat up all the food.

31Then some of the boys He had beaten came and said to Shachi: "Mother, because of your son's prowess we'll probably have to leave the village!

32Your fine little son eats up all the food by force, breaks the dishes, blocks the way of the little ones and thrashes them — he blazes like the submarine fire!"

[p. 17]

33Having heard the children's words, Shachi, threatening, said to her son: "Why do You trouble everyone, You rascal? You don't obey what I tell You!"

34Then the Lord, rubbing His eyes with His little fists, struck His mother with His soft little foot; and the women, catching her, cried out in jest: "Oh, she's been killed!"

35Seeing His mother suddenly fall senseless, Hari grew alarmed. One woman said: "If someone brings coconut water to the one who was struck, she will surely revive."

36No sooner had these pleasant words been spoken than He, eager to bring His mother back to life, went out — and there He stood, having brought a coconut.5

37Seeing this miracle, the brahmin women considered Him superhuman; noticing this, the Lord concealed His greatness under the pretence of singing and dancing.

38Once on the bank of the Ganga He, the golden one, saw some town girls observing a maidens' vow, and with a smile, without a second thought, said to them:

39"To what god in the form of a mantra are all you girls offering worship? Here I am before you, the giver of boons; worship Me, the God above the gods."

40At these words some, feeling dislike, ran away from the place of worship; but others, with tenderness in their hearts, shy and afraid, respectfully worshipped Him.

41Pleased with this, He, an ocean of kindness, gave the girls a fitting blessing: "May wealth, the love of a good husband and seven sons soon come to you."

42And to the girls who had run away He said in play, with a show of respect: "If you go away without worshipping Me, you will surely get an old husband."

43When He said this, one of the flock of girls who had come with offerings — clever in argument, but frightened — suddenly came up to Hari and said:

44"Hey, dear one, you are our brother, since you live in the same town with us! Why do you laugh at us, friend? It's not sensible — with girls…

45Don't curse us: we will worship your feet, tender as shoots, right now." Saying this and casting sidelong glances at Him, they at once began to worship Him.

46Anointed by their worship, the clever one, pleased, at once showered the little girls with many blessings and returned to town as if nothing had happened.6

47One morning the beautiful daughter of the brahmin Vallabha, pure in heart, came to the bank of the celestial river to worship her chosen deity.

48Seeing before Him her with intoxicating eyes, born of a portion of His beloved, devoted to her dear one, the Lord, remembering their former relationship, spoke to her under the guise of a child's mischief:

49"Whom are you worshipping so earnestly, O lovely-eyed one, and for what desire — which celestial — leaving aside Me, the Great Lord who grants desired fruits, here on the bank of the celestial river?"

50Hearing this, she — from the feeling that welled up, from joy at His glance and from childish shyness — at once, glancing sideways, covered her whole face.

51Then these two, who were only pretending to be children, casting off by force the cover made by the art of time, sat rejoicing at heart, exchanging glances full of rasa.

52When Mishra's son, unabashed, quickly removed her veil, she too, unashamed in her childhood, worshipped Him with fragrant flowers and the rest.

53"Today I have learned your desire, sweet one; so it shall be, and not otherwise." Pleasing her with such meaningful words, Hari accepted her offering.7

54Once Shachi went to punish her son for His pranks; and He, fearless, as if frightened, ran far away and sat down in an unclean place.

55Seeing her son touching something unclean, she angrily scolded Him hard: "Bathe! Go into the waters of the Ganga, son, otherwise You may not enter the house."

56Hari, deftly answering His mother's words and as if pointing out the path of liberation, said: "Mother, what have I done? What are you thinking, grieving Me with your words?

57This whole visible world consists of Me; consider in truth: it is not real. Here the activity of the Self appears as transformation, like a conjuror's magic.

58So is there anywhere anything pure or impure? In reality [I am] apart from everything: I, all-pervading, though present [everywhere], am like the sky, distinct from all, unstained."8

[p. 18]

59Hearing these words of the child, full of truth, she grew calm in amazement. And Hari, showing Himself a child, spoke again under the guise of childish mischief.

60Once the father, though he loved his son tenderly, scolded Him for His great mischief and admonished Him with gentle words; and at night both [parents] slept long.

61A certain god, angered, said to him in a dream: "Ah, why do you scold the Great Lord, thinking Him your son? Mishra, your efforts are in vain.

62He who gave the Vedas to the lotus-born, by whose guidance the world continues to exist — to Him you show your authority! You are [as if] showing the wind its way."

63Hearing this, he, without pride, answered the best of the twice-born: "I know that what you say is not false; but the upbringing of a son is the father's duty.

64If the son is well brought up, the father gains fame; if not, he is blamed in the world. This is the father's highest duty; why then do you, not knowing this, speak so?"

65The brahmin at once said to him: "Good Mishra, your words have now revealed your pure parental love; we shall find none equal to it."

66Having thus satisfied each other, these two best of the twice-born gladly ended [their talk]. Then Shachi told her awakened husband what she had seen in a dream about the child:

[p. 19]

67"My lord, some beautiful exalted gods took up the sweetly babbling child and suddenly vanished before the eyes of the townsfolk."

68When she had said this, he, touching her, told her his own dream. Their conversation gave joy not only to them — but also to those who hear [of it].9

69Thus the treasure-house of pastimes, dwelling in Sri Navadvipa-dhama, performed His childhood pastimes, worthy of a wandering Kama; who in the three worlds can sing of all that He did each day, giving joy by [His] deeds?

70And yet, as I heard the truthful account of Him, so, after reflection, I have sung His charming childhood pastimes, abridging them as nectar for the righteous.

71In the Sri Gaura-krishnodaya, composed for the delight of connoisseurs by Govinda — a bee intoxicated by tasting the drops of honey that open within the lotus feet of Sri Gauranga, the bull among the lords of sannyasis — the third canto, devoted mainly to describing His childhood, has come to its close.

72…Meditate on the feet of Sri Gauranga for release from the cycle of births.10

Thus ends the third canto of the Sri Sri Gaura-krishnodaya composed by Sri Govinda.

Notes

  1. CC Adi 13, 14: whenever the women chanted the name of Hari, the crying Infant fell silent; therefore the women chanted constantly around Him.
  2. The clay episode — CC Adi 14: the Lord tells His mother that all food is a transformation of earth, and His mother explains the difference between wholesome and harmful by the example of a clay pot and a lump of clay. Govinda-deva closely retells the CC. The child's words in v. 7 sound like a doctrine of the oneness of all — according to the CC the Lord speaks thus in play and it is His mother who instructs Him; see also note 8.
  3. The pilgrim brahmin (tirthika) — CC Adi 14 (briefly) and in detail the CB, Adi-khanda: three times the Infant eats the food offered to Krishna and reveals to the brahmin His form as Krishna.
  4. The kidnapping of the Infant by thieves for His ornaments — CB, Adi-khanda (two thieves there); briefly mentioned in CC Adi 14. In Govinda-deva there is one thief.
  5. CC Adi 14: angry with His mother, the Lord struck her; she fell unconscious, and the women said she would revive if her son brought a coconut; He at once brought two coconuts. In Govinda-deva, one.
  6. The girls worshipping the gods on the bank of the Ganga, and the Lord demanding worship for Himself — CC Adi 14 (in detail, CB, Adi-khanda). The blessings (a rich, handsome husband, seven sons) and the threat (an old husband) are as in the CC.
  7. The meeting with Lakshmipriya at the Ganga — CC Adi 14: they recognised each other; the Lord demanded worship, and she worshipped Him in her mind. "Born of a portion of His beloved": Lakshmipriya is an incarnation of Lakshmi (GGD). Govinda-deva adds the scene with the veil (vv. 51–52); his epithet "only pretending to be children" stresses that this is the play of eternal consorts, not mundane passion.
  8. CC Adi 14: the Lord sat on discarded pots and, to His mother's reproach, replied that there is neither pure nor impure — all is one (a speech in the manner of the non-dualist doctrine); Shachi in reply explained the rules of purity. According to Bhaktisiddhanta, such words of the child are play, not His teaching: later the Lord Himself refutes the Mayavadis (Madhya 6, 25). In Govinda-deva the words of v. 57, "it is not real" (tan na satyam), are translated literally; the author calls the child's speech "full of truth" (v. 59). What is true in it is that the Lord is all-pervading and unstained (v. 58); but the idea that the world is unreal departs from the teaching of the CC and of Bhaktisiddhanta, according to which the world is a real, though temporary, manifestation of the Lord's external energy, not a deception. In the CC these words of the Lord are play, followed by His mother's instruction.
  9. CC Adi 14: Jagannatha Mishra once scolded his son, and at night in a dream a brahmin rebuked him: "Your son is no ordinary child"; Mishra answered that even if his son is God, a father must bring Him up, and the brahmin praised his love. Shachi's dream (v. 67) is Govinda-deva's addition.
  10. A half-shloka (śrī-gaurāṅga-pada-dvandvaṃ dhyāyatāṃ bhava-muktaye) printed after the colophon stanza as a separate v. 72 (checked against the scan); the edition has no first half.
